newsitem.title: UK: UK takeover watchdog opposes European directive.
newsitem.headline: UK takeover watchdog opposes European directive.

text.p: Alistair Defriez, director general of Britain's Takeover Panel which polices mergers and acquisitions, on Monday underlined his opposition to plans to impose European Union-wide rules on takeover bids.

In an article in Britain's Daily Telegraph newspaper, Defriez said the panel opposed the directive on takeovers, proposed by the European Commission, because "of the damage legislative implementation of it could do to the UK's non-statutory system of takeover regulation".

A framework directive on governing the conduct of company takeovers in Europe was put forward by the commission in February of last year. The Takeover Panel, which works outside a legal framework although its rulings are subject to judicial review, has been vociferous in its argument against the move.
In September the panel again voiced its opposition to the plans, which Defriez said would lead parties in takeovers "to litigate and resort to the courts in ways which are not currently possible".
The directive, which he described as "general, vague and the product of compromise", would not bring any improvement or harmonisation in Europe if implemented, Defriez added.

He said the commission should "address the real barriers to takeover, which deny investors fair treatment and businessmen the level playing field they seek". Defriez highlighted the dismantling of structural and technical barriers and "the encouragement of an equity culture" as the priority.

This, he said, would enable cross-border takeover activity and lead to widely-held and freely-traded equity of the companies involved. Once this was achieved "it might make sense to seek some genuine harmonsisation of takeover regulation".

The current Dutch European Union presidency was unlikely to bring the directive to the Council of Ministers but Luxembourg, which Defriez said had never had a takeover, might do so in the second half of the year, he said.

Defriez said compliance in Britain with the takeover code is virtually 100 percent, adding that since the Panel's foundation in 1968 it has handled over 6,000 offers, and in 1996 dealt with some 200 bids, about a quarter of which were hostile.
"The rest of Europe put together does not have this experience," he said.

But Defriez did not comment in the article on the recent CE Electric bid for British regional electricity company Northern Electric and the role of BZW, the investment banking arm of British bank group Barclays Plc.

The Panel's role in this affair, which ended in Northern losing its independence after the Panel extended the deadline for acceptances in the bitter battle, has come under scrutiny from both the media and market participants.

The decision to allow CE Electric longer to gain acceptances for its hostile bid followed the discovery of an additional fee payment to Northern Electric's adviser BZW late in the process. The panel said BZW should have revealed the fee earlier.

BZW had also bought shares in Northern Electric in the last week of the bid. Although this is allowed to do this under current rules, some commentators have called for a change to the regulations to prevent such support in the future.

BZW's actions are still being investigated by the panel but Defriez has already said that while the Panel would not want to ban advisers from buying shares, it was concerned that purchases should be at arm's length "without any inducement or financial incentive from the target company".
